Board Important – Karnataka 2nd PUC Question Bank

Ecosystem is a compact but very high-yield chapter – ecological pyramids and energy flow questions are asked almost every year, and it's equally important for NEET/KCET.
~8–10 marksSmall chapter, high return – almost every topic yields a guaranteed question
3 × 5 MEcological pyramids (numbers/biomass/energy, upright vs inverted), energy flow & 10% law, decomposition process steps
4 × 3 MStructure of ecosystem (biotic/abiotic), gross vs net primary productivity, standing crop & standing state, carbon cycle
4 × 2 MFood chain vs food web, detritivores vs decomposers, litter, nutrient cycling types

⭐⭐⭐ Top priority – almost always asked (5 marks)

  • Ecological pyramids – numbers, biomass & energy (5 M) – pyramid of numbers is usually upright (grassland ecosystem) but inverted in a tree ecosystem (few trees support many insects); pyramid of biomass is upright in most terrestrial ecosystems but inverted in a pond/aquatic ecosystem (small fish biomass of phytoplankton, but they turn over fast); pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright, since energy decreases at each successive trophic level (10% law of energy transfer, Lindemann 1942).
  • Energy flow in an ecosystem & the 10% law (5 M) – unidirectional flow: solar energy captured by producers (only ~1–5% via photosynthesis) → passed to herbivores → carnivores → top carnivores, with only about 10% of energy transferred to each successive trophic level (the rest is lost as heat/respiration) – this limits food chains to usually 3–4 trophic levels.
  • Steps of decomposition (5 M) – fragmentation (detritivores like earthworms break detritus into smaller particles) → leaching (water-soluble inorganic nutrients percolate into the soil) → catabolism (bacterial/fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances) → humification (leads to formation of dark, amorphous humus, resistant to microbial action, a nutrient reservoir) → mineralisation (humus further degraded, releasing inorganic nutrients).

⭐⭐ High priority – frequently asked (3 marks)

  • Structure of an ecosystem – biotic & abiotic components (3 M) – abiotic (climatic factors like temperature, rainfall, light, and edaphic factors like soil pH, minerals); biotic (producers – autotrophs; consumers – herbivores/primary, carnivores/secondary & tertiary; decomposers – bacteria & fungi).
  • Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) vs Net Primary Productivity (NPP) (3 M) – GPP is the total rate of organic matter production (photosynthesis) by producers; NPP = GPP minus respiration losses (R), i.e. the biomass available to consumers/heterotrophs. NPP = GPP − R.
  • Standing crop & standing state (3 M) – standing crop is the biomass of a species at a particular trophic level at a given time, measured as mass of living organisms (biomass) or number per unit area; standing state refers to the amount of nutrients present in the soil at any given time.
  • Carbon cycle (3 M) – carbon (as CO2) fixed by producers via photosynthesis → passed through the food chain → returned to the atmosphere via respiration, decomposition, and combustion (burning of fossil fuels/wood); the largest carbon pool is oceans, followed by fossil fuels.
  • Litter & the rate of decomposition (3 M) – plant/animal remains (dead leaves, bark, etc.) constitute detritus; the rate of decomposition is controlled by the chemical composition of detritus (rich in lignin/chitin decomposes slowly) and climatic factors (warm, moist conditions favour decomposition; low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit it).

⭐ Two-mark favourites – learn as clean pairs

  • Food chain (linear transfer of energy) vs food web (interconnected network of multiple food chains).
  • Detritivores (organisms that break down detritus into smaller particles, e.g. earthworms) vs decomposers (bacteria/fungi secreting enzymes to digest detritus biochemically).
  • Grazing food chain (starts from living green plants) vs detritus food chain (starts from dead organic matter).
  • Litter – the dead remains of plants/animals on the ground, the starting material for decomposition.
  • Nutrient cycling – gaseous type (reservoir in atmosphere, e.g. carbon, nitrogen cycles) vs sedimentary type (reservoir in Earth's crust, e.g. phosphorus, sulphur cycles).
Answer-writing tip: for pyramid questions, always state explicitly whether each pyramid (numbers/biomass/energy) is upright or inverted AND name the specific ecosystem example (tree ecosystem for inverted numbers, pond for inverted biomass) – a bare diagram without the named exception loses marks.
Never lose these marks: remember the pyramid of energy is the ONLY pyramid that is always upright, never inverted, in any ecosystem – this is a frequently tested trick point.

Ecological Pyramids

Fig 12.1 — Pyramid of Numbers (Upright & Inverted) 5 M ★★★ Top Priority
Draw both side by side: upright pyramid for grassland ecosystem (producers > herbivores > carnivores in number, widest base); inverted pyramid for a tree ecosystem (1 tree supports many insects/birds – narrow base, wider above).
View page 211 in NCERT PDF →
Fig 12.2 — Pyramid of Biomass & Pyramid of Energy 5 M ★★★ Top Priority
Draw the biomass pyramid upright for a terrestrial ecosystem, inverted for a pond ecosystem (small phytoplankton biomass supports larger fish biomass). Draw the energy pyramid always upright – label each trophic level retaining only ~10% of the energy from the level below (10% law).
View page 212 in NCERT PDF →

Food Relationships & Nutrient Cycling

Fig 12.3 — Food Chain vs Food Web 3 M ★★☆ High Priority
Draw a simple linear food chain (grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk) beside an interconnected food web showing multiple chains sharing common organisms, with arrows showing direction of energy flow.
View page 210 in NCERT PDF →
Fig 12.4 — Carbon Cycle 3 M ★★☆ High Priority
Show atmospheric CO2 fixed by producers (photosynthesis) → passed through the food chain → returned via respiration (all organisms), decomposition (decomposers), and combustion (burning fossil fuels/wood); label the ocean as the largest carbon reservoir.
View page 215 in NCERT PDF →
